procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated February 1, 1965 of the Punjab High Court in Criminal Misc. No. 8 of 1964 in Cr. Revision No. 1375 of 1963.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. Criminal proceedings were initiated in the Court of Magistrate First Class, Patiala.
2. Objections were filed before the Magistrate but were overruled.
3. Revision was filed before the Additional Sessions Judge who recommended to the High Court that the criminal proceedings against Kirpal Singh be quashed, but declined to interfere with proceedings against the appellants.
4. Appellants filed Criminal Miscellaneous Petition No. 8 of 1964 in the High Court, seeking consideration of their grounds along with the recommendation for Kirpal Singh.
5. Capoor, J., accepted the recommendation and quashed proceedings against Kirpal Singh, directing the appellants' petition to be placed before another Bench.
6. Sharma, J., dismissed the Criminal Miscellaneous Petition, holding that the points had already been considered and rejected by Capoor, J., in a prior order.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants obtained special leave to appeal the High Court's judgment and order to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the prosecution for offences under ss. 193 and 195, I.P.C., was barred under s. 479A(6), Cr. P.C.

facts: A magistrate acquitted an accused, Bhagwant Rai, and observed that he had been falsely implicated.
The magistrate's successor-in-office later filed a complaint against the appellants for offences under sections 193, 195, 211, and 120B of the Indian Penal Code (I.P.C.).
The appellants argued that the prosecution for the offences under ss. 193 and 195 I.P.C. was specifically barred by section 479A(6) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr. P.C.).
law: The Supreme Court relied on its own previous ruling in the case of *State of Maharashtra and Bahan Singh v. Jagdish Singh*.
application: The Court directly applied the precedent from the *State of Maharashtra* case to the facts of the current case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the appellants' contention, holding that in view of its prior ruling, the prosecution for offences under sections 193 and 195 of the I.P.C. was indeed barred by section 479A(6) of the Cr. P.C.

issue.issue_text: Whether the complaint was properly filed by the successor Magistrate.

facts: A Magistrate's successor-in-office filed a complaint against the appellants for offenses (under ss. 193, 195, 211 I.P.C.) that arose from proceedings before the original Magistrate.
The appellants contended that according to s. 195(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr. P.C.), only the Magistrate before whom the original proceedings took place could file such a complaint.
law: Section 559(1) of the Cr. P.C. states that the powers and duties of a Magistrate may be exercised by their successor in office.
Section 559(2) of the Cr. P.C. provides a mechanism for determining who the successor is when there is doubt.
application: The Court found no force in the appellant's contention, stating that Section 559 of the Cr. P.C. explicitly enables a successor-in-office of a Magistrate to file a complaint.
The Court held that this section applies to all Magistrates and there is no reason to limit its application only to Magistrates of permanent courts.

The Court clarified the role of subsection (2) of Section 559. It explained that this subsection does not limit subsection (1), but rather provides a method to resolve any doubt about who the successor is.

It does not mean that a successor must be formally determined under subsection (2) before they can act. If there is no doubt about the successor's identity, that person can exercise the powers granted by subsection (1).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the complaint was properly filed by the successor Magistrate, as Section 559 Cr. P.C. grants this power to a successor-in-office.

issue.issue_text: Whether the complaint should be quashed on the ground that it was filed due to a private feud and not in the interest of justice.

facts: The appellant's counsel argued that the complaint should be quashed because it was filed due to a private feud between the parties.
law: A legal point or argument generally cannot be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court if it was not raised in the lower courts.
application: The Supreme Court observed that this specific point—that the complaint was motivated by a private feud—was never raised in the High Court at any previous stage of the proceedings.
reasoning.conclusion: Because the argument was being raised for the first time at the Supreme Court level, the Court refused to allow it to be considered and therefore rejected it on procedural grounds.

issue.issue_text: Whether the trial court misconstrued the High Court's remand order.

facts: The petitioners argued that the trial court had misconstrued a prior remand order from the High Court (by Capoor, J.).
They contended that the case was only remanded for trial on offenses under sections 211 and 120-B of the Indian Penal Code, and not for the entire case.
application: The Supreme Court examined the specific text of the High Court's remand order.
The order stated: 'As the order under revision is not legally sustainable, it must be set aside and the respondents must be proceeded with according to law.'
The Court interpreted this language to mean that the "criminal case as a whole was to proceed against all the respondents," not just for the specific offenses mentioned by the petitioners.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the trial court did not misconstrue the High Court's order. The language of the order clearly indicated that the entire criminal case was to proceed, and therefore, the petitioners' argument on this issue was rejected.

issue.issue_text: Whether s. 42 of the Police Act, 1861, barred the prosecution.

facts: The prosecution in the case was for offences under the Indian Penal Code (ss. 193, 195, 211, and 120B), not for an offence under the Police Act, 1861.
law: The court relied on its previous decision in *Mulad Ahmad v. State of U.P.*, which established that the three-month limitation period in Section 42 of the Police Act only applies to prosecutions for acts done under the provisions of the Police Act itself.
Section 42 does not apply to prosecutions for offences committed under other statutes, such as the Indian Penal Code.
application: Since the charges against the accused were under the Indian Penal Code, a separate act, the time limitation specified in Section 42 of the Police Act was not applicable to this case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the prosecution was not barred by Section 42 of the Police Act because the time limit in that section is restricted to offences under the Police Act and does not extend to offences under the Indian Penal Code.

issue.issue_text: Whether the competency of the court to make a complaint under s. 211, I.P.C., could be challenged after the order to file the complaint had become final.

facts: A Magistrate, Shri Joginder Singh, issued an order directing that a complaint be filed against the respondents for several offences, including one under s. 211, I.P.C.
This order directing the filing of the complaint was not appealed by the respondents.
law: An order that is not appealed from becomes final.
application: The Court, citing the holding of Capoor, J., noted that since the Magistrate's order to file the complaint was not appealed, it had become final.
Because the order was final, the competency of the court to make that complaint could not be challenged or considered at a later stage.
The court determined that the issue had already been decided and could not be re-agitated.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the challenge to the competency of the court to file the complaint under s. 211, I.P.C., because the original order directing the complaint to be filed had not been appealed and had therefore become final, precluding any further challenge on that ground.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the prosecution for offences under ss. 193 and 195, I.P.C., was barred under s. 479A(6), Cr. P.C.
appellant_arguments: The prosecution for offences under sections 193 and 195 of the Indian Penal Code was barred by section 479A(6) of the Criminal Procedure Code.
respondent_arguments: The bar under s. 479A, Cr. P.C. did not apply to the entire complaint because two of the offences mentioned, namely under s. 211 and s. 120B of the I.P.C., did not fall within the purview of s. 479A.
The complaint on its face mentions offences under ss. 193, 195, 211 and 120B, I.P.C., and is not limited to only the offences under ss. 193 and 195.
The High Court had ordered that the criminal case as a whole was to proceed against all the respondents, and therefore the case could not be limited to only the offences under ss. 211 and 120-B.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the complaint was properly filed by the successor Magistrate.
appellant_arguments: The complaint could only be filed by the specific Magistrate before whom the original proceedings took place, as per s. 195(1)(b), Cr. P.C.
respondent_arguments: Section 559 of the Cr. P.C. enables a successor-in-office of a Magistrate to file the complaint.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the complaint should be quashed on the ground that it was filed due to a private feud and not in the interest of justice.
appellant_arguments: The complaint was filed because of a private feud and it is not in the interest of justice to allow it to proceed.
respondent_arguments: This point was not raised in the High Court at any previous stage and should not be allowed to be raised now.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the trial court misconstrued the High Court's remand order.
appellant_arguments: The case was remanded only for the trial of offences under sections 211 and 120-B of the Indian Penal Code, not for the case as a whole.
respondent_arguments: The High Court's order stated that 'the respondents must be proceeded with according to law,' which meant the entire criminal case was to proceed against all respondents.

arguments.issue_text: Whether s. 42 of the Police Act, 1861, barred the prosecution.
appellant_arguments: The prosecution was barred by s. 42 of the Police Act, 1861.
respondent_arguments: This ground had already been considered and rejected in a previous order by the High Court and cannot be re-agitated.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the competency of the court to make a complaint under s. 211, I.P.C., could be challenged after the order to file the complaint had become final.
appellant_arguments: The competency of the court to make the complaint should be re-examined.
respondent_arguments: The objections regarding the court's competency had already been heard and finally disposed of in a prior High Court order and cannot be challenged again.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Section 42 of the Police Act, 1861, does not apply to a complaint made by a Court under Section 476 of the Criminal Procedure Code. Furthermore, if there is no doubt as to the identity of a successor judicial officer, that person can exercise the powers of the office without a formal determination process.
obiter: A legal point not taken in the High Court at any stage will not be allowed to be raised for the first time at the appellate stage.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appeal was dismissed because the majority of the appellants' arguments were procedurally barred. The Court refused to consider challenges to the prosecution that had either been finally decided in a prior High Court order and could not be re-agitated, or had not been raised at the appropriate stage in the lower courts. While the Court accepted that the prosecution for offences under ss. 193 and 195, I.P.C., was barred by s. 479A(6), Cr. P.C., this was insufficient to quash the entire proceedings, which were found to have been correctly continued by the trial court based on a proper interpretation of the High Court's remand order.
legal_tests_applied: Principle of Finality: Issues that have been heard and finally disposed of by a competent court in a prior order cannot be re-agitated in subsequent proceedings.
Procedural Bar/Waiver: An argument or point not raised in the lower court cannot be raised for the first time before the appellate court.
Stare Decisis (Binding Precedent): The court is bound by its own previous rulings on a point of law, as seen in its acceptance of the bar under s. 479A(6) based on prior decisions.

Statutory Interpretation: The court interpreted the plain meaning of a judicial order to determine its scope, specifically construing the phrase 'the respondents must be proceeded with according to law' to mean the entire criminal case should proceed.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that the complaint was filed due to a private feud was rejected because: 'This point was not taken in the High Court at any stage and we do not allow it to be raised at this stage.'

The challenge to the trial court's interpretation of the remand order failed because the High Court's order to proceed 'according to law' was interpreted to mean 'that the criminal case as a whole was to proceed against all the respondents.'

The challenges regarding the bar under s. 42 of the Police Act and the competency of the court to file the complaint were dismissed because these objections 'had been heard and finally disposed of by Capoor, J., in his order dated April 4, 1.961' and therefore could not be re-agitated.
The competency of the court to make the complaint under s. 211, I.P.C., could not be challenged because the original order directing the complaint 'was not appealed from and had become final.'
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued that several of the appellant's key objections could not be considered because they had already been 'heard and finally disposed of' in a prior High Court order, which had become final.
The respondent's interpretation of the High Court's remand order was accepted, with the Court finding that the order meant 'the criminal case as a whole was to proceed against all the respondents.'
The respondent successfully blocked a new argument from being introduced at the Supreme Court level by pointing out that it was 'not taken in the High Court at any stage.'
policy_considerations: Judicial Finality: The court reinforced the principle that litigation must come to an end by refusing to allow appellants to re-agitate issues that had already been conclusively decided in prior proceedings.

Orderly Appellate Procedure: By refusing to hear an argument not raised in the lower court, the court upheld the procedural rule that appellate review is limited to issues properly presented and decided below, ensuring a structured and fair judicial process.
